author: Akien
prose:
right so this question points up another thing to me. we have a requirements file now for all intents and purposes. our intentions. many of them have whys. really every one of them needs a why. and every test case where it's not completely f****** clear what it's testing needs a why. if the point is to change the test case, yeah, the why should make that clear and it should be allowed. and all this stuff that's measuring who's doing what, whether it's which builder (they're currently all you) or what is kinda silly. all we care about really is: does it meet the intentions. the inspectors and gates are what should be measuring that: is it clear that this meets the intentions. if we edit the ticket to better meet the intentions, that's nothing but a good thing and it should be supported by downstream activities if the whys make it clear you're not trying to pull a fast one on yourself. see what i mean?

[CC reflected it back; Akien corrected:]

almost: an inspector never adjudicates a why, they're deterministic. but when it fails to pass the gate, then the answer isn't automatically 'it broke, change it' the answer is 'lets check the intentions of the specific sieve and it's why against the ticket's why and see if the ticket is wrong or the sieve' and that check IS done by an LLM after the failure. and it might be long enough to pass one ticket. that ideally would be for things like testing the sieve itself. we can't allow that to be used as a lock pick.
